inclusion.rationale: The study makes dependence in literary text empirically inspectable while remaining separable from the later probabilistic-language-model spine.

significance.beginner: A short literary sequence can reveal that what comes next depends on what came immediately before.
significance.expert: The study estimates conditional vowel/consonant frequencies and compares observed dispersion with independent, simple-chain, and more complex chain assumptions.

limitations: The alphabet is collapsed to the binary classes vowel and consonant, discarding letter identity, words, syntax, and meaning.
The work does not train a predictor or present text generation as its objective.
Markov explicitly says the empirical example may not fully satisfy the theoretical assumptions.
The underlying Pushkin edition, exact terminal character, and a fully reproducible normalization pipeline are not specified.

uncertainties.note: The reviewed primary and historical sources do not document a direct Markov-to-Shannon influence path.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A primary source from Shannon or a participant would need to identify Markov’s text study as an influence.

inclusion.rationale: The paper brings discrete stochastic sources, conditional sequence probabilities, entropy, and constructed English approximations together in one inspectable formal account.

significance.beginner: Changing how much earlier text affects the next choice changes both the appearance and predictability of generated symbol sequences.
significance.expert: The paper represents written language as a discrete stochastic source, develops finite-state and n-gram conditionals, and relates longer contexts to conditional source entropy.

limitations: The paper is an engineering theory of communication and explicitly brackets semantic meaning from that engineering problem.
The English sequences are illustrative samples constructed from letter and word frequency information and book-based successor sampling, not learned neural models or evidence of comprehension.
Many discrete-source results use finite-state models and, unless stated otherwise, an ergodicity assumption; these idealizations should not be universalized.

inclusion.rationale: The paper turns contextual next-character predictability into an explicit experiment and connects ranked predictions to entropy bounds.

significance.beginner: A guessing experiment makes it possible to feel how preceding text narrows the plausible next character.
significance.expert: The paper estimates conditional character entropy from human rank predictions, separates observed prediction from an ideal conditional-probability ranking, and derives upper and lower bounds.

limitations: The experiments use human next-character prediction, not a trained language model, next-word task, or free-running generator.
The main context experiment draws from one literary source, permits reference aids, and does not report participant demographics or variability.
The long-context estimates use smoothed samples and apply an ideal-predictor lower bound to human rankings with an explicit approximation caveat.

uncertainties.note: The paper’s reported long-context condition and its N versus N-1 indexing should be preserved rather than silently normalized.

inclusion.rationale: Good’s paper publishes the frequency-of-frequencies estimate and unseen-mass identities that Katz later cites and adapts. It is represented as context because its main formulation concerns species-frequency estimation rather than a conditional language model, even though the paper names literary vocabulary as another application.

significance.beginner: The number of types seen once can tell us something about how much probability may still belong to types never seen at all.
significance.expert: Good expresses low-frequency probabilities through smoothed frequencies of frequencies, credits Turing for the central adjusted-count formula, and derives represented mass near 1 − n₁/N with unseen mass near n₁/N.

limitations: The paper’s primary formulation concerns species in a population, not conditional word-sequence probabilities or a language-model decoding system.
Good explicitly credits A. M. Turing for formula (2); representing the published paper as a work node does not make Good the sole originator of the estimator.
The adjusted-count formula is meant to use smoothed nᵣ values; substituting raw, sparse frequency-of-frequency counts without that caveat can produce unstable or undefined estimates.
The paper does not contain Katz’s history-conditioned normalization, zero-estimate gate, or recursive lower-order m-gram backoff.

uncertainties.note: The article itself attributes formula (2) and a large share of the credit to A. M. Turing while publishing the derivation and broader treatment under Good’s sole authorship.

bibliography.citation: F. Jelinek, L. R. Bahl, and R. L. Mercer, “Design of a Linguistic Statistical Decoder for the Recognition of Continuous Speech,” IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 21(3), 250–256 (May 1975).

versions.notes: The manuscript-received day and the May 1975 journal issue are recorded as separate chronology events. The IBM archive’s 1 January catalog date is not used for ordering.

inclusion.rationale: The paper formulates a modular, corpus-estimated word-sequence probability within a factorized speech-decoding objective. It belongs as an engineering integration point on the statistical-ASR branch without being treated as the sole hinge in that broader line of work.

significance.beginner: When speech sounds are ambiguous, the decoder combines how well a candidate matches the sounds with how plausible its word sequence is in the domain.
significance.expert: The maximum-a-posteriori decoder factors Pr(W|A;L) into a language-model probability Pr(W|L) and a front-end likelihood Pr(A|W;L), then searches finite-state hypotheses by likelihood.

limitations: The article specifies a decoder that the IBM group planned to implement; it does not report end-to-end recognition accuracy or an experiment isolating the language-model contribution.
The target is carefully spoken speech in a relatively noiseless environment, with a roughly 10,000-word vocabulary and a two-million-word corpus of laser patent applications.

The decoder begins from a phonetic-symbol string supplied by a separate, speaker-trained acoustic processor rather than learning directly from waveforms; pronunciation and phonological probabilities are also speaker-dependent.
The instantiated language model uses explicit recent-word, part-of-speech, and content-class state features rather than learned distributed representations.
The paper leaves probability estimation for unseen language-model transitions under investigation.

Partial-hypothesis likelihoods use an approximation, and the described decoder scores the best state path while assuming that the loss relative to marginalizing all paths for a word sequence is negligible.
The work concerns speech transcription and does not present the language model as a standalone text generator.

uncertainties.note: The paper uses an information-theoretic framing but does not cite Shannon’s 1948 or 1951 papers; the atlas therefore records mechanism continuity without asserting paper-specific influence.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A source explicitly naming Shannon’s 1948 or 1951 paper as an influence would be required to document a paper-specific path.

uncertainties.note: The explanatory weight of this design article relative to its companion 1975 channel-decoding paper and Jelinek’s broader 1976 treatment has not yet received a claim-level comparison.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: Compare the three primary texts before considering whether one should represent the statistical-ASR branch as a core hinge.

versions.notes: The proceedings year is supported at year precision. The workshop dates belong to the volume title; the paper’s presentation day and a more precise proceedings publication date have not been established.

inclusion.rationale: The paper turns sparse Markov transition estimation into an explicit prediction problem, combines detailed and tied estimates by interpolation, and develops held-out and deleted procedures for testing the combination on data treated as unseen. It belongs as a statistical-estimation branch without being treated as a text-only or neural language model.

significance.beginner: A transition missing from a finite sample is not necessarily impossible, so the estimator blends a specific but fragile estimate with a broader estimate whose evidence is stronger.
significance.expert: The paper linearly interpolates detailed and tied Forward–Backward transition estimates, fits reliability-dependent weights on held-out or deleted blocks, and gives fixed and relaxed deleted-interpolation procedures.

limitations: The method is formulated for general finite-state Markov sources, including null transitions; the paper does not present the recursive higher-order-to-lower-order word n-gram equation commonly associated with later Jelinek–Mercer language-model smoothing.
The model structure and state-tying design are supplied by the experimenter, while the paper notes that a real generator’s structure is normally unknown and can be too large.
The held-out split size, deletion-block length, occupancy thresholds, state tying, and initial transition distributions are unresolved design choices that depend on the modeled situation.

The fixed deleted procedure uses a computational shortcut whose component estimates still depend implicitly on all data; the paper says separate per-block Forward–Backward runs would avoid it at higher cost.

The abstract reports simulations and successful speech-process applications, but the chapter gives no simulation table, dataset specification, quantitative comparison, or recognition metric from which to reconstruct those results.
The work estimates finite-state transition probabilities and does not learn distributed representations or a standalone text generator.

uncertainties.note: The National Diet Library record and the inspected chapter give pp. 381–397, ending with the complete reference list. J-GLOBAL additionally indexes pp. 401–402, whose content and relation to the chapter were not available for inspection.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: Inspect the complete proceedings volume at pp. 398–402 to determine whether pp. 401–402 are discussion pages associated with this contribution.

uncertainties.note: The 1980 bibliography does not cite the 1975 decoder paper; it cites a different, then-forthcoming chapter by Jelinek, Mercer, and Bahl. The atlas therefore relates the two works editorially rather than as documented paper-specific influence.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A contemporary citation or participant source explicitly connecting the two papers would be required to upgrade the relationship evidence class.

uncertainties.note: The abstract’s simulation and speech-application claims cannot be evaluated quantitatively from the inspected chapter.

inclusion.rationale: The canonical chapter applies sparse-transition interpolation to a named trigram language model, reports how often unseen trigrams recur in new text, and gives a concrete deleted-estimation procedure. It supplies a word-trigram instantiation of the general 1980 estimator while remaining a broad speech-recognition survey rather than a standalone general-purpose language-model paper. Claim-level comparison found the same eight promoted lineage claims in the differently titled 1983 journal article, so that publication is recorded as a companion version rather than a second lineage node.

significance.beginner: Even a corpus of 1.5 million words leaves plausible three-word patterns unseen, so the chapter blends a fragile specific estimate with a broader one and chooses the balance using text treated as new.
significance.expert: The chapter maps the sparse-data failure to an IBM Laser Patent Text trigram model, applies equation (8.1) to detailed and tied transition estimates, and estimates reliability-bucketed mixture weights by deleted blocks.

limitations: The concrete language-model example is the domain-specific IBM Laser Patent Text corpus inside a continuous-speech-recognition survey; it is not evidence about unrestricted modern text.
The reported 23% unseen-trigram share is not reconstructible from the chapter passage because the new-text sample, its size, and the evaluation protocol are not specified there.

Equation (8.1) blends detailed and tied transition estimates; the inspected section does not present the compact recursive trigram-to-bigram-to-unigram notation associated with later descriptions of Jelinek–Mercer smoothing.
The chapter discusses a statistical language component within a larger speech system and does not learn distributed representations, semantics, or long-context dependencies.
The chapter is a broad survey of the IBM continuous-speech-recognition program; its atlas inclusion is limited to the sourced trigram and deleted-interpolation bridge.

Grouping the differently titled 1983 article, with its different author order, as a companion version is an editorial deduplication choice. It does not assert that the authors or publishers designated it as an edition, reprint, or derivative.

versions.title: Learning Distributed Representations of Concepts
versions.label: Original Cognitive Science Society proceedings paper

bibliography.citation: G. E. Hinton, “Learning Distributed Representations of Concepts,” in Proceedings of the Eighth Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society, pp. 1–12, Amherst, Massachusetts, 1986.
bibliography.venue: Proceedings of the Eighth Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society

versions.notes: The official program supplies the scheduled presentation date of 15 August 1986; the proceedings publication itself is dated only to 1986. The eScholarship record’s normalized January date and 2024 repository-ingest date are not treated as publication events. No DOI or open-content license was verified.

inclusion.rationale: The paper supplies a concrete, inspected example in which a network learns internal distributed codes from relational propositions and uses their geometry to generalize within a small structured domain. Bengio et al. later cite this work when describing learned distributed representations for symbolic data. It is retained as a representation-learning precursor, not as a language model or a claim of priority for distributed representations, backpropagation, or modern word vectors.

significance.beginner: Neutral person and relation symbols are translated into learned compact patterns whose similarities reflect useful family-tree regularities, allowing some unseen relations to be completed without hand-written semantic features.
significance.expert: A deterministic feed-forward sigmoid network learns separate six-unit role-specific codes for person and relation inputs, exposes isomorphic family structure in those codes, and tests four withheld relation instances across two random initializations.

limitations: The experiment uses two synthetic isomorphic family trees, 24 people, 12 relation types, and 104 relation instances; four facts are withheld and the same entities, relations, and templates remain in training.

Only two random initializations are reported: one network answers 4 of 4 held-out facts correctly and the other answers 3 of 4. There is no baseline, confidence interval, significance test, or broader held-out study.
The paper describes the chosen layered family-task architecture as somewhat arbitrary and demonstrates only one feasible design, not the best or only design.
The architecture is feed-forward, not recurrent, and its role-specific six-unit codes are not one shared modern word-embedding table.
The word-form analogy is explicitly limited: lexical ambiguity such as bank would require phrase or sentence context that the simulation does not model.
The author says there is no domain-independent prescriptive theory of sensible generalization; the reported result is bounded to particular structured domains.
The learned-unit interpretations are qualitative readings of weights rather than quantitative disentanglement measurements, and sex is omitted from one code because it is redundant for the task.
The family relations encode binary-sex and heteronormative assumptions that require historical contextualization.
The paper calls major aspects of the learning procedure biologically implausible; the paper and complete proceedings have no verified open redistribution license.

uncertainties.note: The day-level ordering represents the scheduled conference presentation, while proceedings publication remains at year precision.

bibliography.citation: S. M. Katz, “Estimation of Probabilities from Sparse Data for the Language Model Component of a Speech Recognizer,” IEEE Transactions on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing, vol. 35, no. 3, pp. 400–401, March 1987.
bibliography.venue: IEEE Transactions on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing
bibliography.publisher: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers

versions.notes: The article is ordered by its March 1987 journal issue. Crossref’s day-valued license-start field and its 2004 DOI-registration date are not treated as publication dates; the printed article supplies the author’s full name and manuscript history.

inclusion.rationale: The article gives a compact, explicit account of discounting low-count m-grams, reserving probability mass for unseen events, and conditionally falling back to normalized lower-order distributions. It also contrasts this nonlinear backoff construction with Jelinek–Mercer deleted estimation. The work is retained as a classical statistical-language-model branch rather than evidence about neural representation learning or long-context modeling.

significance.beginner: A rare phrase should not consume all the model’s trust, and an m-gram should not be treated as impossible solely because it was absent at the current order. Katz discounts uncertain observed counts, keeps probability in reserve, and uses a broader lower-order pattern when the more specific estimate is zero.
significance.expert: The estimator combines adjusted low-count Turing coefficients, an explicit unseen-mass budget, and a zero-estimate gate that rescales the recursively defined lower-order conditional distribution by α; counts above k are left undiscounted.

limitations: The article is a two-page treatment of an m-gram component for IBM speech recognizers; it does not model distributed representations, semantics, or dependencies beyond the chosen finite context.

The recursion uses a lower order when the higher-order estimate is zero rather than linearly mixing every order; the paper separately reports an optional d₁ = 0 space-saving variant that deliberately makes singleton estimates zero.
The article attributes its frequency-of-frequencies estimator to Turing through Good’s 1953 paper and explicitly locates its own novelty in nonlinear backoff, not in Turing’s formulas.

Table I reports one 100-sentence test on models estimated from approximately 750,000 words of office correspondence, without vocabulary, tokenization, split, uncertainty, or implementation details sufficient for reproduction.
The recommendation that k be about five and the assertion of weak sensitivity to the discount coefficients are practical statements without a displayed sensitivity analysis.
The institutionally hosted scan retains an IEEE copyright line and has no verified open license; it is used for inspection and is not redistributed.

uncertainties.note: The article states that its novelty lies in the nonlinear backoff procedure with explicit unseen-mass estimation, not in the use of Turing’s formulas.
The paper does not specify enough experimental detail to reconstruct the three Table I model implementations or assess variation beyond the reported perplexities.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: Locate a contemporary experiment report, implementation description, or archived model configuration giving the corpus split, vocabulary, preprocessing, estimator settings, and repeated evaluation.

uncertainties.note: No publisher-authorized open full text or author-hosted copy was identified; the inspected university-hosted scan is not treated as evidence of redistribution permission.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A rights-holder statement or explicitly licensed repository copy would be required to classify the article as open full text.

versions.title: Finding Structure in Time
versions.label: Canonical Cognitive Science journal article

bibliography.citation: J. L. Elman, “Finding Structure in Time,” Cognitive Science, vol. 14, no. 2, pp. 179–211, March 1990.

versions.notes: Wiley and Crossref support March 1990 and the current DOI. The ScienceDirect legacy publisher record associates the same article with Cognitive Science 14(2), April–June 1990, and DOI 10.1016/0364-0213(90)90002-E; both DOI identifiers remain attached to this single journal version. The separate 1991 Machine Learning article on simple recurrent networks and grammatical structure is not a version of this work.

inclusion.rationale: The work connects next-item prediction, carried hidden state, and emergent task-dependent internal structure in inspected sequence experiments. Its simple recurrent architecture is a consequential precursor for recurrent modeling, while Bengio et al. later cite the journal article specifically for learned distributed representations of symbolic data. The record keeps those two contributions distinct and does not recast the experiments as a normalized language model.

significance.beginner: A copy of the previous hidden pattern lets the same current item produce different predictions after different histories, and learning to predict the next item organizes hidden states without supplying word-class labels.
significance.expert: The architecture copies hidden activation one-for-one through fixed unit-weight links, trains the remaining paths with local next-step error, and reports task-dependent lexical-state geometry and successor-frequency fit on controlled generated sequences.

limitations: The hidden-to-context copy connections are fixed at weight 1.0; only the input/context-to-hidden and hidden-to-output paths are trained. The article does not describe full backpropagation through earlier copied states.

The lexical experiment uses 29 words in 10,000 generated two- and three-word sentences, orthogonal one-hot 31-bit inputs, 150 hidden units plus 150 context units, and six passes; it is not a natural-corpus language-model evaluation.
The paper inconsistently reports 27,534, 27,354, and 27,454 words for the lexical corpus. These source counts remain unresolved and are not normalized into one value.
Network output activations need not sum to one. The reported successor-frequency comparison is not a normalized softmax distribution, likelihood objective, or perplexity evaluation.

Averaging a word’s hidden states across contexts can create a clustering artifact because preceding contexts are category-dependent; the described token-level check is not displayed and has no quantitative clustering metric.
The memory is practically bounded by finite numerical precision, repeated nonlinear transformation, exponential decay, and delayed-error training; representational capacity remains open.

The experiments report no seed count, confidence intervals, recurrence ablation, modern baseline, natural-language-scale syntax test, or reproducible implementation, and the conclusions are described as preliminary.
The unavailable superseded 1988 report cannot support journal-specific technical claims, and its abstract mentions a pronominal-reference simulation absent from the inspected 1990 article.

inclusion.rationale: The work supplies an inspected neural natural-language-processing system in which error-driven learning updates a global distributed word lexicon shared by recurrent modules for sentence-role and scripted-story tasks. Bengio et al. cite it as an earlier neural language-modeling example while explicitly contrasting its word-role objective with their normalized word-sequence distribution. The branch preserves that historical connection without relabeling FGREP or DISPAR as a probabilistic language model.

significance.beginner: Several small recurrent networks learn meaning-like patterns for words in one shared lexicon, then pass those patterns between sentence and story tasks. The system learns expectations and scripted completions, but it does not assign a normalized probability to each possible next word or sentence.
significance.expert: FGREP extends backpropagated error into globally stored input/output word representations, while DISPAR chains four separately supervised recurrent FGREP modules around a shared lexicon. The audited manuscript reports synthetic case-role and script-paraphrase metrics and explicitly frames its probabilistic behavior as weighted-average output patterns rather than an explicit sequence distribution.

limitations: The claim-located reading copy is an author-hosted 46-page prepublication manuscript with internal pp. 1–46, not the publisher’s pp. 343–399 journal layout; technical locators and manuscript-specific wording are not transferred to unseen journal pages.

The experiments use generated sentence templates and nine stereotyped restaurant, shopping, and travel story templates rather than a natural text corpus.

The four DISPAR modules are trained separately with compatible intermediate targets; during training, imperfect upstream outputs are replaced by correct patterns from the current lexicon rather than propagated end to end.

An external supervisor supplies fixed role and script slots, module-level targets, sequence segmentation, and execution control. The paper treats automatically discovering intermediate targets and neural control as future work.
The internal representation uses a fixed number of assemblies, cannot naturally represent an unbounded number of fillers, and is optimal only for the task that developed it.

The strong incomplete-story completion behavior depends on low variation and deliberately stereotyped scripts; the authors report poor handling of exceptions and little extrapolation beyond training regularities.
The reported percentages have no confidence intervals, significance tests, repeated-seed analysis, or comparison with a normalized statistical language model.

inclusion.rationale: The paper makes the lower-order distribution itself an object of estimation for unseen m-grams. Its distinct-context and singleton-count solutions explain why raw lower-order frequency can be a poor fallback signal and provide a major classical backoff node; the later interpolated and modified variants are recorded as a separate, sourced extension.

significance.beginner: A word that is frequent in only a few fixed phrases should not automatically look likely after every unseen context. The fallback distribution asks how broadly a word continues different contexts, not only how often it appears.
significance.expert: The paper preserves a normalized seen/unseen backoff form and optimizes its lower-order distribution in two ways: the marginal-constraint path yields distinct-context counts under absolute discounting, while a separate leave-one-out path yields singleton-event counts.

limitations: The paper is a four-page ICASSP treatment whose main Verbmobil and Wall Street Journal comparisons use trigram language models; its final ARPA comparison adds one bigram row, and it does not model distributed representations, semantics, or long context.

The marginal derivation treats the denominator in equation (6) as constant with respect to the predicted word, and the leave-one-out derivation makes an analogous approximation to the second sum in equation (16).
The simple distinct-context result assumes nested history classes, reliable coarse marginals, one unique coarser class for each detailed history, and a single absolute discount with 0 < d < 1.

The experiments use nonlinear interpolation from Ney, Essen, and Kneser 1994 as a slight variant of absolute discounting for seen events, and smooth every backoff distribution by an unspecified method to avoid zero probabilities.

The paper does not present the later interpolated Kneser–Ney formulation or modified Kneser–Ney’s count-dependent D₁, D₂, and D₃₊ discounts; the separate Chen–Goodman record must not be projected backward into its equations.
The abstract’s claim of perplexity improvements up to about 10% is approximate: Table 1’s compact marginal-constraint row changes from 169.4 to 150.6, an 11.1% relative reduction.
The reported 5% word-error improvement is an approximate relative summary, not a five-percentage-point reduction: the best full WSJ row changes from 11.9% to 11.1%.
No significance analysis, confidence interval, runtime benchmark, measured memory footprint, discount-tuning procedure, complete preprocessing description, or test-set size is reported.

inclusion.rationale: The report versions and journal article isolate exponentially unstable or decaying temporal error flow, construct a unit-weight recurrent state path, and regulate storage and access with learned multiplicative gates. This supplies the recurrent-memory branch later applied to word language modeling, while its evidence remains bounded to artificial long-lag tasks and its cell predates the learned forget gate and cell-state-to-gate connections used in later systems.

significance.beginner: A memory cell keeps one internal value on a fixed recurrent loop, while learned input and output gates decide when new information may enter and when stored information may affect the network. This makes long-delayed learning signals easier to preserve, but it does not make every long-memory problem easy.
significance.expert: The architecture creates a constant error carousel through a unit-weight self-connection, learns multiplicative input and output gates, and uses a spatially and temporally local truncated-gradient algorithm. Its synthetic experiments include minimal lags above 1,000 steps, while the discussion preserves delayed-XOR, parity, capacity, counting, and parameter-overhead boundaries.

limitations: All reported experiments use generated artificial sequences; speech processing, time-series prediction, and music are future applications rather than evaluated evidence.

The efficient algorithm deliberately truncates error flow when it leaves memory cells or gate units. The paper says strongly delayed XOR-like tasks may require a full gradient, while also reporting that its few non-truncated trials did not materially differ.
Table 3’s thousand-step results concern a two-class trigger-and-distractor task with error only at sequence ends, not natural language, continuous discourse, or real-world memory.
Each memory-cell block adds input and output gate units. The discussion bounds dense-network weight overhead and notes capacity, precise counting, parity, and internal-state-drift problems.
The original cell has input and output gates but no learned forget gate or cell-state-to-gate feedback links; those later modifications must not be projected backward into this work.
The inspected report versions and journal text provide no code or code link, learned parameters, data generator package, hardware-normalized timing, or modern replication protocol.

versions.title: Learning to Forget: Continual Prediction with LSTM
versions.label: Canonical Neural Computation article

bibliography.citation: F. A. Gers, J. Schmidhuber, and F. Cummins, “Learning to Forget: Continual Prediction with LSTM,” Neural Computation, vol. 12, no. 10, pp. 2451–2471, 1 October 2000.

versions.notes: The publisher record supplies journal metadata and article history. The inspected author-hosted reading copy has one acceptance cover followed by stable internal pages 1–19; those internal pages support technical locators but do not map to the published folios 2451–2471.

inclusion.rationale: This work isolates a failure of the original constant-error cell on unsegmented continual streams and adds an adaptive forget gate that learns when to retain, decay, or reset state. It is the documented bridge from the 1995/1997 input/output-gated cell to later composite LSTM variants, while its evidence remains synthetic and version-specific.

significance.beginner: The original memory cell could keep adding small values until its state became unusable unless someone reset it at known boundaries. A learned forget gate lets the cell keep useful state, fade it, or clear it from the data itself.
significance.expert: A block-shared sigmoid gate replaces the CEC’s fixed unit self-weight in the state recurrence, and its eligibility trace is reset when the gate closes. Continual embedded-Reber and noisy temporal-order experiments test learned segmentation and reset, with exact protocol, success-rate, and version boundaries preserved.

limitations: All evaluated problems are generated sequence tasks; the paper does not test language modeling, natural speech, or a real-world continual stream.
The topology is not optimized, and the main continual experiments use 100 independently initialized networks without confidence intervals, formal significance tests, or a modern replication package.
The state-decay comparison reports one selected fixed decay value and does not provide a broad matched hyperparameter search.

The continual direct baselines are omitted where the authors say those methods already fail easier component tasks; the paper therefore does not provide a complete matched baseline table for every continual condition.

The ICANN paper covers only the continual embedded-Reber experiment. The technical report and journal add the continual noisy temporal-order task, and their Table 3 mean training counts differ materially; results are never transferred silently across versions.

The author-hosted February report build prints a different forget-weight derivative term from the later institutional build and journal equation. Promoted mechanism and learning-rule claims use the audited journal version.
The paper’s ‘forgetting’ resets recurrent activation state; it is not evidence about catastrophic forgetting of learned parameters.
Public reading copies and records provide no verified paper-level open-content license, so this repository links rather than redistributes the full texts.

inclusion.rationale: The work supplies the explicitly cited neural joint-distribution mechanism that the later neural probabilistic language model adapts: an ordered product of conditional distributions whose constrained hidden units share computation across predictions. Its separate NIPS, IDIAP, and IEEE records preserve the 1999 conference event and distinct 2000 publication artifacts without treating bibliographic suffixes as chronology or asserting a direction among the companion treatments.

significance.beginner: A huge table of every possible variable combination becomes a sequence of smaller questions. A constrained neural network answers those questions while reusing hidden features, so evidence from observed combinations can inform combinations the data did not contain.
significance.expert: The model applies an order-sensitive chain factorization, parameterizes normalized conditionals with triangular grouped connectivity and shared deterministic hidden units, grows as O(n²H) under its stated construction, and trains by likelihood or MAP; its pruning rule and four-dataset likelihood study expose both the intended capacity control and its empirical limits.

limitations: The model operates on fixed-dimensional vectors of variables; it does not itself implement variable-length language modeling or time-shared next-word prediction.
The variable order is chosen rather than learned, and the approximation can change when that order changes.
General marginalization can require a combinatorial sum; missing values are tractable only in restricted cases described by the authors.
The connectivity-pruning procedure uses pairwise Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests and a cross-validated threshold, so it is a heuristic rather than a search over all higher-order dependencies.
The empirical study covers four UCI or STATLOG tabular density-estimation tasks and negative log likelihood; it does not establish language-model, classification, or outlier-detection performance.
The paired test described by the authors conditions on the learned model and does not include variability from selecting a different training set.
The NIPS and repository-manuscript result tables differ slightly for pruned LARC, so numerical values remain version-specific.
The official and institutional reading copies are publicly accessible, but no paper-level open-content license was verified and no PDF is redistributed by this repository.

versions.label: ICSLP 2000 proceedings paper

bibliography.citation: W. Xu and A. Rudnicky, “Can Artificial Neural Networks Learn Language Models?,” in 6th International Conference on Spoken Language Processing (ICSLP 2000), vol. 1, pp. 202–205, 2000.
bibliography.venue: 6th International Conference on Spoken Language Processing (ICSLP 2000)

versions.notes: The official archive supplies vol. 1, pp. 202–205, DOI, and the October 16–20 conference span. The exact presentation day is not identified, so chronology remains at month precision.

inclusion.rationale: The paper evaluates a normalized neural next-word distribution against Katz, Jelinek–Mercer, and Kneser–Ney baselines on a spoken-dialog domain, making it an explicit probabilistic language-model branch. Bengio et al. describe the proposal as independent and identify its no-hidden-unit, single-input-word boundary. The record therefore preserves both the direct softmax-bigram contribution and the sharp separation from later learned word representations and multiword predictors with an optional hidden path.

significance.beginner: A network receives the current word and produces a probability for every possible next word. Held-out early stopping is intended to limit overfitting before the table converges to unsmoothed empirical bigram frequencies, but the experiment never learns word features or uses more than one previous word.
significance.expert: A one-hot V-input/V-output affine softmax with V(V+1) parameters is trained by batch backpropagation on negative log likelihood from zero initialization and selected by held-out perplexity. The class-based Communicator experiment narrowly edges the listed Kneser–Ney row, while the paper’s linear analysis shows that its simple early-stopping interpolation is inadequate and leaves the full softmax model’s implicit smoothing form unknown.

limitations: The implemented model has no hidden units and receives one input word, so it captures only unigram and bigram statistics and learns no distributed word representation.

The Communicator domain has an approximately 2,500-word vocabulary represented by about 1,200 language-model classes, including 20 multiword classes; reported perplexities exclude within-class probability.

Table 1 contains one train/holdout/test split from one spoken-dialog domain, with no confidence intervals, significance tests, repeated seeds, speech-recognition error rate, or out-of-domain evaluation.
The neural test perplexity of 11.16 differs from the listed Kneser–Ney value of 11.17 by 0.01, and the no-OOV values differ by 0.10; these rows do not establish broad superiority over count models.
The Jelinek–Mercer row omits a no-OOV value, and the paper does not report split sizes, class-frequency details, OOV counts, or enough preprocessing information for reproduction.

The authors’ simplified linear early-stopping derivation performs poorly at 19.24 test perplexity. They infer that the experimental softmax network smooths frequent and infrequent events differently but state that its exact interpolation form is unknown.
Training takes about one minute per epoch for thousands of epochs on a Pentium III 500 MHz machine, compared with less than half a minute to obtain the paper’s Katz or Jelinek–Mercer model.
Hidden units, additional history, recurrent connections, another domain, and long-distance dependencies are future work rather than properties of the evaluated system.
The official archive provides public reading access but no verified paper-level open-content license; the PDF is linked and not redistributed by this repository.

versions.notes: This canonical version adds Christian Jauvin, uses Brown and Associated Press News corpora, expands the fixed-window architecture, optimization, parallel implementation, baselines, ablations, and limitations, and records submission in April 2002 and publication in February 2003.

inclusion.rationale: The work trains jointly learned continuous word representations and a normalized neural next-word distribution in experiments reaching a 17,964-word vocabulary and a 13,994,528-word training stream. The authors position this as pushing an acknowledged prior idea to large scale; its controlled Brown comparisons expose the roles of context, hidden units, and a count-model mixture, making it the atlas’s audited neural-language-model turning point without treating the Transformer as the beginning.

significance.beginner: Instead of storing every phrase as an unrelated case, the model learns a reusable vector for each word and a predictor that can transfer probability behavior across nearby vectors. The paper’s implemented model still sees only a fixed number of previous words.
significance.expert: The canonical model concatenates shared lookup-table vectors for an n−1-word context, applies optional hidden and direct paths, normalizes the full vocabulary with a softmax, and jointly optimizes embeddings and predictor parameters by penalized likelihood. Its results and compute profile expose both the representational gain and the full-softmax bottleneck.

limitations: The canonical experiments use a fixed n−1-word window; recurrent architectures are discussed as an allowed implementation and future direction, not evaluated as the main model.
One vector represents every occurrence of a word, which the authors identify as a poor fit for polysemy.
Full-vocabulary normalization dominates computation: for the Associated Press configuration, weighted sums feeding the output units account for about 99.7% of the estimated numerical operations.
The strongest Brown result, test perplexity 252, includes a fixed mixture with an interpolated trigram; the corresponding neural model without that mixture reports 276.
The paper’s statement that the best n-gram is 24% above the best neural result compares 312 with 252; it is not a 24% baseline-relative perplexity reduction, which is about 19.2%.

The Associated Press comparison reports 109 for the neural/trigram mixture and 117 for the strongest listed modified Kneser–Ney baseline; the baseline-relative reduction is about 6.8%, although the paper summarizes the gap as about 8%.
The Associated Press run stopped after five epochs, took approximately three weeks on 40 CPUs, and showed no signs of overfitting on the validation set according to the authors.
Evaluation is limited to English next-word perplexity on Brown and Associated Press News splits, with no downstream task, confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple-seed analysis.
The JMLR paper explicitly says neural language models were not new and cites earlier examples; the corpus does not assign it sole priority for the idea.
The NeurIPS and JMLR versions differ in authors, datasets, architecture variants, baselines, and results, so numerical claims are not transferred between them.
The official reading copies are publicly accessible, but no explicit Creative Commons license was verified and the corpus does not redistribute them.

inclusion.rationale: The paper explicitly extends the Bengio approach cited in its reference [1] into a 64,000-word continuous-speech recognizer, estimates the full-output bottleneck, and evaluates a 2,000-word neural shortlist with reuse of sequential same-context decoder requests. significance.beginner: A neural next-word model is placed inside a speech recognizer, but it scores only a frequent-word shortlist and lets the existing backoff model handle everything else. Repeated requests for the same context reuse one cached prediction, turning an otherwise impractical calculation into a decoder experiment.
significance.expert: The paper jointly learns shared word projections and a tanh-softmax predictor, quantifies the hypothetical 64k full-output cost, preserves backoff shortlist mass in a normalized hybrid, and reuses shortlist outputs across sequential same-context requests during HUB5 decoding. Perplexity gains survive broadcast-news interpolation, while WER changes remain small and explicitly inconclusive.

limitations: The selected system normalizes neural probabilities over a static 2,000-word shortlist rather than the full 64,000-word recognition vocabulary; the backoff model supplies all remaining-word probabilities and the shortlist’s total probability mass.

The parameter paragraph prints n=2 even though the paper repeatedly calls the models 3-grams and explicitly defines their history as the two previous words; the context length is clear, but the symbol n is overloaded or used inconsistently.
Switchboard1 contributes 248 hours and CallHome English 17 hours, totaling 265 hours, while the paper describes the acoustic data as about 280 hours.
Only 46.6% of requested decoder probabilities use the network, so the reported recognition experiment is a hybrid coverage result rather than full neural replacement of the language model.

The WER changes are 0.5 percentage points without acoustic adaptation and 0.3 percentage points with adaptation, with no confidence intervals, significance tests, repeated runs, or end-to-end runtime.
The paper’s 4.9% perplexity-reduction entry for 138.8 to 132.4 differs from the roughly 4.6% reduction calculated from the displayed values.

Reference [1] omits Pascal Vincent, supplies no pages, and prints Morgan Kaufmann although the authoritative volume publisher is MIT Press; its distinctive title, volume 13, year, and retained authors nevertheless resolve it to the existing three-author NeurIPS conference version.

versions.label: JMLR article

bibliography.citation: F. A. Gers, N. N. Schraudolph, and J. Schmidhuber, “Learning Precise Timing with LSTM Recurrent Networks,” Journal of Machine Learning Research, vol. 3, pp. 115–143, August 2002.

versions.notes: The official record and complete 29-page PDF identify one JMLR version with printed folios 115–143. Printed p. 115 says Submitted 5/01, Revised 3/02, and Published 8/02; only publication controls ordering because the schema does not relabel the paper’s ‘Submitted’ notation as a received date. The legacy DOI 10.1162/153244303768966139 currently resolves to a deleted-record tombstone and is not an active identifier for this version.

inclusion.rationale: The paper explicitly builds on forget-gated LSTM and adds learned cell-state-to-gate peephole connections so gates can inspect a protected timer. It separates retention control from state visibility and provides timing-task experiments and ablations that make the later composite LSTM used for language modeling historically traceable.

significance.beginner: A closed output gate can hide a cell’s internal timer from the other gates. Peephole connections let the gates inspect that protected state directly, while the separate forget gate still decides when the timer should be cleared.
significance.expert: Input and forget peepholes read the previous cell state, while the output peephole reads the newly updated state, fixing the gate-update order. The paper adds three weights per cell under its one-cell setup and tests precise timing through missing-symbol, spike-generation, and no-input waveform tasks.

limitations: The experiments use bespoke synthetic timing tasks, one memory block with one cell, ten independently initialized networks, thresholded success criteria, roughly tuned momentum, and early stopping; no natural-language task is evaluated.
The paper’s tables compare its forget-gated LSTM with and without peepholes but do not include an ordinary recurrent-network control, despite broader claims about traditional recurrent networks.
The authors report no clear statistical advantage for peepholes on the missing-symbol task overall; stronger evidence is specific to generated spikes and nonlinear periodic functions.
The learning procedure truncates gate errors and does not propagate gate error backward through peepholes into the constant-error carousel, so gating is not fully recurrent.

The evaluated cell shares gates across a block, omits the common output-state squashing function, and uses customized truncated RTRL/backpropagation; it is not identical to every later ‘standard LSTM’ shorthand.
The paper identifies capacity, modularization, nontrivial stack or queue behavior, noisy temporal triggers, and zero-state initialization as unresolved boundaries.
The legacy Crossref DOI record is deleted and carries incorrect year, volume, journal, and ISSN metadata; it is retained only as version-boundary evidence and must not be displayed as an active DOI.
The paper is publicly readable and retains author copyright, but no article-specific open-content license was verified.

bibliography.citation: T. Mikolov, M. Karafiát, L. Burget, J. Černocký, and S. Khudanpur, “Recurrent neural network based language model,” in Interspeech 2010, Makuhari, Japan, pp. 1045–1048, September 2010.

versions.notes: The official archive supplies the DOI, pp. 1045–1048, and the September 26–30 conference span. The full text retains the printed proceedings folios, so claim locators use those pages.

inclusion.rationale: The paper explicitly combines the simple recurrent architecture it attributes to Elman with the normalized neural word-prediction problem it contrasts with Bengio’s fixed-window model, then evaluates that combination at speech-recognition scale. It is promoted as a convergence milestone for practical recurrent word language modeling and online adaptation, with its contribution bounded to that documented combination and evaluation.

significance.beginner: Instead of showing the network a hard window of recent words, the model carries a changing state from one word to the next and turns that state into a probability distribution for the following word. The repeated state can carry information beyond a fixed window, but the paper itself says this simple recurrent model still fails to capture truly long context reliably.
significance.expert: A one-hot word vector and the preceding sigmoid state are concatenated into an Elman-style recurrence, followed by a vocabulary softmax and cross-entropy training. The experiments use one-step truncated temporal credit assignment, rare-word bucketing, linear interpolation with modified Kneser–Ney models, RNN ensembles, and optional test-time SGD adaptation across WSJ and RT05 rescoring conditions.

limitations: The evaluated training uses a temporal depth of one: error is propagated only from the current time step, and the authors explicitly call this non-optimal.
The conclusion says the simple recurrent model did not capture truly long context; a cache remained complementary even to dynamically adapted models.
Words below a frequency threshold are merged into one rare token, and its probability is divided uniformly among the rare word types rather than learned separately for each one.

The larger recurrent models can require several weeks of training, and the WSJ recurrent models use at most 6.4 million words while some count-model comparisons use 37 million; the paper does not supply controlled hardware-normalized throughput.

The strongest WSJ results depend on ensembles, interpolation with modified Kneser–Ney models, dynamic test-time updates, or combinations of those components rather than a single static recurrent model.

The Table 3 dynamic evaluation entry is 16.3 with a superscript footnote marker, not 16.34; the footnote says the evaluation sentences are not consecutive and offers that fact as a probable explanation for the worse dynamic-than-static result.

inclusion.rationale: The paper applies a gated recurrent memory cell to word language modeling, evaluates it against a sigmoid recurrent model, studies projection and output-factorization choices, and carries the model into large-vocabulary speech rescoring. It joins the recurrent-language-model and gated-memory branches while preserving the short paper’s limited experimental detail.

significance.beginner: A recurrent language model uses distinct controls for writing, retaining, exposing, and inspecting stored state. On the paper’s word-prediction tests this composite cell lowers perplexity, and when mixed with a much larger count model it lowers the two reported speech-recognition error rates by 0.5 and 0.3 percentage points.
significance.expert: The system combines the original constant-error and input/output-gated core with the 1999/2000 forget gate and 2002 cell-state-to-gate connections, plus a vocabulary softmax, optional input projections, and class-factored output normalization. Penn Treebank comparisons, long-context concatenations, output clustering, and French 1000-best rescoring expose both gains and reproducibility boundaries.

limitations: The fixed-window versus full-history contrast is conceptual: the experiments do not establish usable unlimited context, and the paper’s average sentence length of 21 words is not a maximum context bound.

The evaluated cell is composite. It retains the constant-error, input-gate, and output-gate core from the cited 1997 article while adding a forget gate and cell-state-to-gate connections. The target collectively assigns those modifications to references 12 and 13; a cross-source audit maps the forget gate to the 1999 paper and the weighted state-to-gate ‘peepholes’ to the 2002 paper. Sundermeyer et al. do not use the term peephole, reproduce the earlier equations, or prove implementation identity.

Penn Treebank results are plotted rather than tabulated, so most exact perplexity points, context-length curves, and clustering values cannot be recovered reliably from the paper; the text also does not identify whether Figure 3 reports development or test perplexity.
The reported roughly eight-percent perplexity advantage compares LSTM and sigmoid recurrent models in this paper; it is not a numerical reproduction of Mikolov et al. 2010.
Longer concatenated context eventually worsens perplexity, and the prose and graph do not fully agree about the sigmoid-projection curve.
Class factoring displays a large speed increase and a small perplexity loss, but the paper gives no numeric graph table, hardware specification, wall-clock duration, or end-to-end latency.
The French experiment reports only interpolation with a much larger Kneser–Ney model, not an LSTM-only result or a French sigmoid-recurrent comparison.

inclusion.rationale: The preprint unifies character-level recurrent generation, mixture-density handwriting prediction, and text-conditioned handwriting synthesis. Its differentiable Gaussian-mixture window supplies a documented monotonic alignment precursor that Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio later compare directly with their non-monotonic source weighting, while its evidence and terminology remain bounded to the target text.

significance.beginner: A recurrent model predicts text or pen motion one step at a time, then a moving soft window lets typed characters guide generated handwriting without a supplied character-to-pen alignment. The window can glide only forward, which is useful for writing order but restrictive for tasks that must revisit or reorder source positions.
significance.expert: The paper combines stacked peephole LSTMs, normalized categorical or mixture-density next-step likelihoods, and an unnormalized sum of Gaussian window weights over a character sequence. Exponentiated positive location increments impose monotonicity; conditional negative log-likelihood trains the coupled network, and revision-specific corrections bound the gradient equations.

limitations: The work is an arXiv preprint; no inspected record establishes a peer-reviewed conference or journal publication for this title.
The text results mix static and online-adapted evaluation, and the Hutter comparison notes that PAQ-8 includes executable code and is not directly equivalent.
The supplied text samples are qualitative; the paper explicitly says the model loses coherence beyond short phrases and that dynamic adaptation can contaminate later samples with recent topics.

The handwriting experiments use the official IAM-OnDB test partition as additional training data and reserve only the smaller validation partition for early stopping, leaving no independent test set for the reported log losses.

The 31.3-nat log-loss improvement compares adaptive weight noise with the otherwise matched unregularized conditional network and comes with no significant sum-squared-error change; it measures regularization rather than the window. The separate 44% sum-squared-error reduction compares the conditional networks with the best prediction-only network and is not a window-only ablation.

The author says presentation-based blind taste tests suggested that at least some unbiased samples could not be distinguished from real handwriting, but supplies no participant count, protocol, uncertainty estimate, or released judgments. Only Figure 18's primed samples are explicitly selected for legibility; the other displayed figures remain qualitative without a stated selection protocol.
The window is an unnormalized positive weighting function rather than a probability distribution, and its cumulative positive location increments require left-to-right monotonic traversal.
Biased sampling is a temperature-like heuristic that narrows mixture components; it is not a maximum-a-posteriori decoder.
The paper calls the device a window or convolutional mechanism, not attention. Later terminology is used only when describing later sources that explicitly compare it.
The arXiv non-exclusive distribution license permits arXiv hosting but does not establish an open-content reuse license; this repository links rather than redistributes the PDFs or datasets.

uncertainties.note: All five arXiv revisions were compared. The first posting already contains the monotonic soft window; later versions clarify prose and correct equations rather than introducing the mechanism.

Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio explicitly describe Graves’s Gaussian window and its monotonic-location restriction, but do not say their method was derived from it. The relationship therefore records a documented comparison and prohibits a causal claim.
No independent test-set result, released training code, random-seed report, or reproducible protocol was located for the handwriting experiments.

inclusion.rationale: The work defines a jointly trained variable-length encoder–decoder conditional model, contributes reset/update gated recurrence, and evaluates neural phrase-pair probabilities inside a large phrase-based translation system. It is a core branch toward sequence transduction and later attention while its actual evidence remains phrase-table scoring rather than end-to-end sentence translation.

significance.beginner: One recurrent network compresses a variable-length phrase into one vector and a second unfolds a target phrase one word at a time. Reset and update controls let each unit decide what prior state to ignore or carry, while the experiment keeps this neural score inside an existing phrase-based translator.
significance.expert: The model maximizes conditional sequence log-likelihood through a fixed-vector encoder and autoregressive softmax decoder. Equations 5–8 define the reset/update gated unit; the WMT’14 evaluation uses 1,000-unit encoders and decoders, rank-100 word projections, a maxout output path, 15,000-word vocabularies, and phrase-table feature integration rather than direct sentence-level decoding.

limitations: The encoder exposes the source only through one fixed-length vector; the paper does not offer a per-output mechanism for revisiting individual source positions.

The quantitative evaluation scores phrase pairs already present in a conventional phrase table. Replacing the table and generating full translations with the neural model are future work, not evaluated results.

The 15,000-word vocabularies cover about 93% of the selected data and collapse every other word into one unknown token, so an individual out-of-vocabulary word receives the aggregate unknown probability.
The strongest test row combines the encoder–decoder feature with a separate continuous-space language model; it does not isolate a standalone neural translation system.
The ungated tanh observation is described as preliminary and has no controlled protocol, table, repeated seeds, or uncertainty analysis.
The phrase and word plots are qualitative two-dimensional projections; they supply no cluster metric or held-out representation test.
The June preprint and canonical proceedings paper report different baseline and result tables. Values remain attached to their source version.
No confidence intervals, statistical tests, repeated-seed results, released model, or complete end-to-end runtime are reported.

versions.notes: The latest official arXiv revision is canonical because the aggregate record resolves to it. It restores several yᵢ₋₁ indices and a missing W in the appendix, but a separate sᵢ versus sᵢ₋₁ output inconsistency remains; it is not treated as a globally corrected decoder specification.

inclusion.rationale: The work replaces one source summary shared by every target prediction with a decoder-conditioned soft weighting over position-wise bidirectional annotations. It connects the fixed-vector encoder–decoder branch to later attention-based sequence modeling while providing a scoped WMT’14 comparison and unusually interpretable, though only qualitative, alignment visualizations.

significance.beginner: Instead of forcing every translated word to rely on the same whole-sentence summary, the decoder forms a fresh view of the source at each step. It scores all source positions, turns those scores into weights, and blends bidirectional annotations so the visible focus can move as the translation unfolds.
significance.expert: A bidirectional encoder yields hⱼ; a learned feedforward alignment score eᵢⱼ = vₐᵀ tanh(Wₐsᵢ₋₁ + Uₐhⱼ) is normalized across source positions, and cᵢ = Σⱼαᵢⱼhⱼ conditions the autoregressive decoder. The paper trains this differentiable path jointly under translation likelihood and compares RNNsearch with a fixed-context RNNencdec family on WMT’14 English–French.

limitations: The fixed-vector bottleneck is presented as a conjecture. The experiment changes attention, bidirectionality, and model capacity together and supplies no component-only or parameter-matched ablation.
Only WMT’14 English-to-French is evaluated, so the paper does not establish generalization across language directions, tasks, or streaming settings.
The full-test neural results trail the Moses baseline; the strongest comparison with Moses occurs only on a filtered no-unknown subset and after substantially longer training.
Moses uses an additional 418M-word monolingual corpus, while the neural models use the selected parallel data, so the system comparison is not data-matched.
No multiple seeds, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or parameter-matched attention-only and bidirectionality-only ablations are reported.
Figure 2 omits numeric length-bin values, bin construction, sample counts, and uncertainty; its curves support a descriptive result rather than a reconstructible statistical analysis.
The four attention matrices in Figure 3 are conditioned qualitative examples. The paper reports no gold alignment metric, human alignment assessment, or causal intervention on the weights.
Global source scoring performs one alignment evaluation for every source–target position pair, and the authors identify this TₓTᵧ cost as a possible limit outside typical translation lengths.
Separate 30,000-word vocabularies map all other tokens to one unknown symbol; rare and unknown word handling remains an explicit future challenge.
The seven public revisions contain material decoder-indexing and missing-matrix inconsistencies. The atlas does not silently synthesize a detailed gate equation across versions.

The paper omits a random seed, beam width, length normalization, exact BLEU command, length-bin construction, and ordinary-run checkpoint rule, so the reported table is not exactly reproducible from the paper alone.
The arXiv record grants repository distribution rights rather than a permissive content license; the atlas links the paper and redraws concepts instead of assuming reuse rights for its figures.

uncertainties.note: Version 7 is the latest official arXiv revision and canonical technical record, while version 6 is the closest public snapshot before the ICLR presentation. Canonical status does not imply that every appendix indexing inconsistency was corrected.

Bahdanau version 1 publicly preceded Sutskever version 1 by nine days but already cited an anonymized Sutskever manuscript, and Sutskever version 1 reciprocally cited Bahdanau. This establishes prepublication cross-awareness, not conception, submission, private-circulation, or influence order.

significance.beginner: A deep LSTM reads a whole source sentence into one vector, then a second LSTM writes a translation word by word until an end token. Reversing only the source sentence moves several corresponding early words closer in the training computation and makes the optimization easier.
significance.expert: Equation 1 factorizes a target sequence under a softmax LSTM language model initialized by the encoder’s final state. The evaluated system uses separate four-layer, 1,000-cell encoders and decoders, limited vocabularies, gradient clipping, length-bucketed minibatches, multi-GPU training, left-to-right beam search, reversed sources, and five-model ensembles on WMT’14 English–French.

limitations: The source is represented by one fixed-dimensional final state. The model has no mechanism for consulting different source positions during individual target predictions.
The 34.81 direct-translation result uses an ensemble of five reversed-source LSTMs and beam size 12; it is not a single-model or unreversed result.
Source and target vocabularies are limited to 160,000 and 80,000 words, with every other type mapped to one unknown token; the reported BLEU score is penalized by uncovered reference words.
The long-sentence conclusion comes from one sorted/binned figure and examples under the reversed-source ensemble. It does not establish unbounded memory or remove the fixed-vector bottleneck.
The PCA plots use a small selected set of phrases and provide qualitative structure without a representation metric or held-out invariance test.
Beam search is approximate, and the paper specifies no length normalization; beam-size comparisons do not establish globally optimal sequence decoding.
The strongest reranking row combines the neural score with an existing phrase-based system’s 1,000-best list, while the strongest direct row depends on ensembling.
The proceedings paper supplies no confidence intervals, statistical tests, repeated aggregate variance, released model, or complete preprocessing implementation.
The official proceedings and arXiv version 3 disagree on 380 versus 384 million parameters and the latter alone prints an 8,000-dimensional state description; these details remain version-bound.
The official pages provide public reading access but no verified paper-level open-content license; the PDFs are linked and not redistributed by this repository.

uncertainties.note: The official schedule establishes a 9 December 2014 oral presentation, while the public arXiv version appeared on 10 September and remains the ordering event.

Version 1 explicitly describes the work as parallel to Cho et al. and calls the fixed-vector strategy independently taken; later versions omit that wording. The relationship is therefore represented as a noncausal conceptual parallel, not a priority or derivation claim.

The target uses the LSTM formulation from Graves while citing Hochreiter and Schmidhuber for the architecture. The lineage edge does not import the original 1995/1997 equations or claim implementation identity.

Reference 30 names Sundermeyer, Schlüter, and Ney’s LSTM language-model paper but prints 2010 rather than its verified 2012 Interspeech date. Title and authors resolve it to the existing corpus work; the erroneous year is not propagated.
No explicit open-content license was found for the canonical proceedings full text.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A rights-holder statement or licensed repository copy would be required before classifying or redistributing the PDF as open content.

bibliography.citation: S. Sukhbaatar, A. Szlam, J. Weston, and R. Fergus, “End-To-End Memory Networks,” in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 28, pp. 2440–2448, 2015.
bibliography.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems
bibliography.series: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems

versions.notes: The official nine-page main paper uses visible article pp. 1–9 while the volume assigns pp. 2440–2448. Its two-page official supplement is incorporated into arXiv version 5; canonical main-text claims use article pagination.

inclusion.rationale: The work makes repeated content-addressed reads from an explicit memory differentiable from answer or next-token supervision, applies those reads to question answering and language modeling, and is named in the Transformer’s final background as a recurrent-attention precedent outside sequence-aligned recurrence. It is a memory-and-attention branch, not an origin claim for self-attention or large-scale language models.

significance.beginner: The story context does not have to be compressed into one hidden state or matched to one fact. The model embeds the question as one query vector, softly weighs stored items, blends what it retrieves, updates the query, and can look again before answering; because every choice remains soft, the final answer error can teach the retrieval steps.
significance.expert: MemN2N computes pᵢ = softmax(uᵀmᵢ), o = Σᵢpᵢcᵢ, and repeated state updates before a cross-entropy output. Adjacent or layer-wise tying, position and temporal encodings, and end-to-end gradients turn explicit memory access into a recurrent computation, with bounded QA and word-LM evidence rather than demonstrated recurrence-free or large-memory scaling.

limitations: The first three revisions use the title Weakly Supervised Memory Networks and contain only the bAbI question-answering treatment; language-model claims begin in the retitled fourth revision.
Removing supporting-fact labels does not make training unsupervised: answers and next-token targets still provide cross-entropy supervision.
The bAbI benchmark contains synthetic language and a 50-sentence memory cap; the model still fails several tasks and does not match the strongly supervised Memory Network baseline.
The language-model study uses finite memories up to 200 words, selects Penn Treebank results across ten initializations, and reports only one Text8 training run.
The strongest language-model rows use different hidden widths and parameter counts from the cited baselines; no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.
More hops improve the aggregate comparison and best listed settings, but individual task and perplexity rows are not monotonic with every added hop.
Table 1 reports 12.4% for the highlighted 1k joint PE+LS+RN system while the surrounding prose says 12.6%; the atlas preserves the table value and the conflict.
The supplement’s nonlinear task-17 result is printed as 18,6 and remains above the paper’s 5% failure threshold even though the accompanying footnote says added nonlinearity solves tasks 17 and 19.

The final paper says ten QA runs were selected by lowest training error while 10% of training data was held out to choose architectures and hyperparameters; it does not fully specify how those two selection stages interact.
The authors explicitly warn that smooth lookups may not scale to larger memories, so the phrase possibly large external memory is architectural framing rather than demonstrated scalability.

The architecture is recurrent attention over an external memory, not Transformer-style self-attention, parallel sequence mixing, multi-head attention, or evidence that Transformer positional encoding came from this work.
Public arXiv and NeurIPS access does not establish a permissive paper-level reuse license; diagrams should be redrawn rather than copied without a qualifying permission.

uncertainties.note: One arXiv identifier groups the title and scope change: the immutable first three PDFs say Weakly Supervised Memory Networks, while versions 4–5 and the proceedings paper say End-To-End Memory Networks.
The official nine-page paper and two-page supplement correspond to the eleven-page arXiv version 5 body and appendices, apart from publication layout and appendix-versus-supplement cross-references.
No explicit open-content license was found for the canonical proceedings paper.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A rights-holder statement or licensed repository copy would be required before treating the paper’s prose or figures as openly reusable.

bibliography.venue: Proceedings of the 2015 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing

versions.notes: The ten-page official article retains printed pp. 1412–1421 and names Minh-Thang Luong even though the Anthology metadata shortens the first name to Thang. Its malformed concat-score display, equation numbering, unqualified local differentiability wording, and omitted p = 0.2/D = 10 details remain canonical-version boundaries rather than being silently corrected from arXiv v5.

inclusion.rationale: The paper systematically compares global and local cross-attention, dot, bilinear, additive, and location scores, and input feeding in a common large-scale translation system. It supplies the unscaled dot-attention bridge and practical local-window branch later contrasted with the Transformer, while remaining an explicitly recurrent encoder–decoder rather than self-attention.

significance.beginner: The decoder can inspect every source position, inspect only a small predicted neighborhood, or remember its previous focus by feeding the last attentional summary into the next step. Comparing those choices reveals what attention changes without treating one heatmap or ensemble score as proof of a universal mechanism.
significance.expert: Luong et al. factor the decoder through h̃ₜ = tanh(Wc[cₜ;hₜ]), compare location, dot, bilinear general, and additive concat scores, introduce differentiable local-m/local-p windows and attentional input feeding, and audit them on WMT English↔German. The unscaled multiplicative score is technically adjacent to later scaled dot-product attention, but the Transformer’s dot-product paragraph does not cite Luong.

limitations: The model remains a four-layer recurrent LSTM encoder–decoder, so training and generation retain sequence-aligned recurrence even when attention consults source states.

The five-BLEU headline compares a reverse-plus-dropout baseline at 14.0 with a local-p/general/input-feeding system at 19.0; it is not a clean local-window-only ablation, whose marginal step after global input feeding is 0.9 BLEU.
The 25.9 WMT’15 result is NIST BLEU from a heterogeneous eight-model ensemble plus unknown-word replacement, not one attention architecture or one model.
The German-to-English system reaches 24.9 BLEU after unknown replacement but remains below the cited 29.2 phrase-based and 27.6 NMT systems.
Only selected score-and-window combinations were run; two local-m dot runs exceed perplexity 7 and report no BLEU, while concat results are limited to perplexity.
The length analysis gives plotted buckets without counts, exact points, uncertainty, or a component-matched causal control.
Alignment error rate uses forced reference decoding and one selected source link per target, while the Berkeley comparator uses one-to-many links and an additional one million WMT sentence pairs.
The official proceedings equation for the concat score is malformed or underspecified; the corrected vₐᵀtanh(Wₐ[hₜ;h̄ₛ]) form, dropout p = 0.2, and D = 10 occur only in arXiv version 5.
The official paper calls local attention differentiable, whereas arXiv version 5 narrows the claim to differentiable almost everywhere and describes the Gaussian as truncated.

The paper reports single training trajectories without seed lists, uncertainty intervals, or significance-test details; code and models are linked without immutable revision or checkpoint identifiers in the paper.

Transformer cites the paper as part of recurrent encoder–decoder progress, but its scaled-dot-product section does not cite Luong; technical continuity does not establish direct adoption or invention of dot-product attention.
ACL licenses pre-2016 Anthology material under CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 while excluding third-party content; arXiv’s non-exclusive distribution license is not a general permission to reuse its assets.

uncertainties.note: The paper PDF and all arXiv versions name Minh-Thang Luong, while ACL metadata normalizes the first author to Thang Luong; the canonical work follows the authored full text and records the metadata difference.

The official ten-page proceedings paper and the eleven-page arXiv version 5 are separate evidence versions. Their September records overlap at the available precision, so the atlas does not infer their within-month public order; version-5 corrections and Appendix A do not transfer into the proceedings text.
