bibliography.venue: Proceedings of the 2016 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing

versions.notes: The official eleven-page article uses printed pp. 551–561, retains the version-6/7 result family, and links the author repository recorded separately with its current access status. Canonical claims use the proceedings folios; revision-only claims use article pagination.

inclusion.rationale: The paper places a differentiable attention read over a growing tape of prior recurrent states inside each LSTM update, then combines that intra-sequence read with cross-sequence attention through shallow and gated deep fusion. It supplies a recurrent intra-attention branch explicitly cited in the Transformer background, without equating its sequential memory update with recurrence-free Transformer self-attention.

significance.beginner: Instead of asking one LSTM state to summarize everything read so far, the reader keeps a tape of earlier hidden and memory vectors. Each new word softly chooses which earlier entries matter before the recurrent gates write the next state; for sentence pairs, another attention stream can consult the other sentence.
significance.expert: LSTMN scores prior hidden states with the current input and preceding adaptive summary, uses the resulting distribution to read aligned hidden and cell tapes, and substitutes those summaries into the gated recurrent update. Shallow fusion composes intra-attentive encoder and decoder modules with cross-attention; deep fusion recurrently stores the source summary through an additional gate.

limitations: Every token update remains sequential and conditions on earlier adaptive recurrent state; the architecture is not a recurrence-free all-position sequence mixer.
The work concentrates on attentive reads from the tape and leaves attention-controlled writes to future investigation.

The tape is said to grow until an upper memory-span bound, but the bound and eviction or truncation rule are not specified; table phrases such as memory size 300 refer to vector dimensionality rather than a documented slot cap.
Despite its machine-reading framing, the paper evaluates language modeling, sentiment, and natural language inference rather than a question-answering or reading-comprehension benchmark.
Its induced token relations receive only task-level supervision, remain soft and undirected, and are illustrated with selected examples rather than evaluated against structural annotations.
The language-model, sentiment, and inference studies use three bounded datasets and selected comparator families; they provide no repeated-run variance, confidence intervals, or statistical tests.
The strongest canonical SNLI system has a reported count of 3.4 million parameters, substantially more than several listed recurrent comparators, which the authors caution limits direct comparison.

ArXiv result tables change materially: version 3 reports 92.3/89.1 for deep fusion, versions 4–5 report an improved 92.1/89.0 variant, and versions 6–7 plus the proceedings omit that variant without explaining its removal.
The two LSTMN sentiment rows change from 49.3/87.3 and 49.8/87.9 through version 5 to 47.6/86.3 and 47.9/87.0 in versions 6–7 and the proceedings without an explanation.
The paper-linked SNLI-attention repository returned HTTP 404 when checked on 23 August 2026; its recorded URL therefore supplies no currently accessible immutable code revision or checkpoint.

Transformer includes Cheng in the grouped prior self-/intra-attention task citation whose first listed context is reading comprehension; that context does not establish adoption of the recurrent memory tape, its gated fusion equations, or its empirical results.
ACL states that 2016-and-later Anthology material is CC BY 4.0 while excluding third-party content; any atlas diagrams should still be redrawn and attributed.

uncertainties.note: No inspected primary source explains why the improved SNLI row or the earlier sentiment rows disappear or change in later revisions.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A dated author correction, review record, or version note would be needed to characterize the reason rather than only the observed textual boundary.

versions.notes: The official seven-page article uses printed pp. 2249–2255 and matches arXiv version 2’s corrected intra-attention denominator. Its PDF prints Ankur P. Parikh while the Anthology metadata shortens the given name to Ankur; the authored full text controls the canonical author list.

inclusion.rationale: The paper factors cross-sentence soft alignment into independent attend, compare, and aggregate computations, producing an attention-only textual-entailment system whose core avoids recurrent and convolutional encoders. Its optional feed-forward intra-sentence attention adds only bucketed relative-distance bias. The Transformer cites this recurrence-free attention case in its background, but the citation does not establish direct mechanism adoption.

significance.beginner: The model aligns each word or local phrase in one sentence with a soft blend from the other, compares every aligned pair separately, then sums those local judgments before classifying the sentence pair. The optional same-sentence pass adds a small notion of distance without requiring recurrent reading order.
significance.expert: Shared feed-forward F projections turn every cross-sentence pair into a dot score, bidirectional softmaxes form aligned phrases, shared G networks compare each pair, and H classifies the sums. The optional F_intra self-alignment concatenates a distance-biased same-sentence mixture; total work is O(ℓd² + ℓ²d), parallel over positions, and O(ℓd²) only under the paper’s ℓ < d assumption.

limitations: The vanilla model intentionally uses no word-order information; the optional variant supplies only learned relative-distance buckets and still fails selected sequence-sensitive cases.

The O(ℓd²) simplification depends on the paper’s ℓ < d assumption, illustrated by SNLI lengths below 80 and cited LSTM hidden dimensions of at least 300; the paper reports no measured latency or hardware speedup.

The printed multi-class cross-entropy expression lacks the conventional leading minus sign in both arXiv revisions and the proceedings article, while the text calls it a loss without specifying whether the displayed quantity is maximized or minimized.
ArXiv version 1 prints d_(i−j) in every denominator term of equation 7; version 2 and the proceedings correct the summation term to d_(i−k).
The 86.8 test accuracy is one half percentage point above the listed 86.3 systems, with no repeated-run variance, confidence interval, or significance test.
The nearly one-order parameter comparison applies to the 382K vanilla model versus the 3.4M Cheng comparator; the 582K intra-attention system is about 5.8 times smaller, excluding embeddings.
Training uses ten asynchronous update threads, selects the best development checkpoint across 50 million steps, and provides no seeds, immutable code, checkpoints, or run-level uncertainty.
Table 3 contains selected examples rather than an aggregate error taxonomy; all compared systems miss highlighted antonym, numerical, and sequence-sensitive cases.

Transformer cites the work as an attention-only textual-entailment case; that context does not establish adoption of its attend–compare–aggregate factorization, distance bias, SNLI training recipe, or results.
ACL states that 2016-and-later Anthology material is CC BY 4.0 while excluding third-party content; any atlas diagrams should still be redrawn and attributed.

uncertainties.note: The authored proceedings PDF and both arXiv versions print Ankur P. Parikh; the ACL record shortens the name to Ankur Parikh. The work and canonical version follow the full text.
No inspected primary source explains whether the missing minus sign in the displayed cross-entropy expression is typographical or reflects an implicit maximization convention.

versions.title: Attention Is All You Need
versions.label: Canonical NIPS 2017 proceedings paper

bibliography.citation: A. Vaswani et al., “Attention Is All You Need,” in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30, pp. 5998–6008, 2017.
bibliography.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems
bibliography.series: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems

versions.notes: The official 11-page PDF is canonical. It consistently reports 28.4 English–German and 41.0 English–French BLEU and omits the arXiv parsing section, parameter-attention appendix, and attention-visualization appendix. Technical locators use its visible article pp. 1–11, not volume folios 5998–6008.

inclusion.rationale: The work makes self-attention the principal sequence-mixing operation in both halves of an autoregressive encoder–decoder, combines it with scaled dot products, multiple learned projection heads, explicit position signals, and position-wise computation, and reports a parallelizable training path with strong translation results. It is an architectural convergence point rather than an origin claim for attention, self-attention, encoder–decoders, or autoregressive generation.

significance.beginner: Every token can build a fresh weighted view of other permitted positions instead of waiting for a recurrent state to travel step by step. Several heads make different projected views in parallel, position signals preserve order, and a causal mask keeps the decoder from seeing future target tokens.
significance.expert: Six-layer encoder and decoder stacks combine residual connections followed by layer normalization, multi-head scaled dot-product self- and cross-attention, position-wise ReLU networks, sinusoidal input positions, tied embeddings/output weights, masked autoregressive decoding, Adam warmup, label smoothing, and byte-pair or word-piece vocabularies.

limitations: The architecture removes sequence-aligned recurrence and nontrivial-width convolution from its sequence-mixing layers, not all non-attention computation: it retains embeddings, position-wise feed-forward layers, residual paths, layer normalization, and a softmax output.
Training-time token representations can be computed in parallel within a layer, but ordinary target generation remains autoregressive and therefore sequential across output positions.
Full self-attention has quadratic O(n²d) layer cost. The proposed restricted alternative for long inputs is future work rather than an evaluated remedy in this paper.

Table 1 is an asymptotic operation and path-length analysis, not empirical evidence that shorter paths alone improve learning on long dependencies; the paper reports no length-stratified translation test.

Table 2 compares systems with different data, model families, hardware, training recipes, and ensemble conditions. Its training costs are estimates from time, GPU count, and assumed sustained FLOP rates rather than matched wall-clock measurements.

The strongest translation rows use checkpoint averaging, development-tuned beam search and length penalty, and different English–German versus English–French setups. They do not isolate a single architectural component.

Table 3 reports one English–German development condition without seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several rows change dimensions or parameter counts, and the 0.9-BLEU single-head gap does not establish a universal advantage for any number of heads.

The attention visualizations are selected qualitative examples. They provide no gold syntax or coreference evaluation, representativeness protocol, human assessment, or causal test that attention weights are faithful explanations.

The constituency-parsing experiment and visualization appendix occur in the arXiv family but are absent from the canonical proceedings PDF; their claims and locators cannot be transferred into that version.

The arXiv revisions disagree on English–French BLEU and training time: version 2 has three different values or conditions, version 3 retains a body/table mismatch, and versions 5–7 print 41.8 in the abstract and table but 41.0 in Section 6.1.
The NeurIPS landing-page metadata has a stale abstract with 165 million parameters and 27.5/41.1 BLEU, while the linked canonical PDF reports 28.4/41.0; technical claims follow the PDF.
The paper links Tensor2Tensor code but identifies no immutable commit, released checkpoints, random seeds, or fully pinned data and preprocessing artifact for exact reconstruction.

The paper’s Cheng and Parikh citations establish recurrent intra-attention and attention-only textual-entailment context, respectively; they do not establish direct adoption of either predecessor’s equations, architecture, training recipe, or results.

NeurIPS says authors retain copyright and grant the venue a non-exclusive publication license. ArXiv versions 6–7 add narrower permission to reproduce tables and figures with attribution for journalistic or scholarly works; the atlas links the sources and does not infer a general open-content license.

uncertainties.note: All seven arXiv revisions and the separate proceedings PDF were compared. The core architecture is already present in version 1, the output projection and several clarifications arrive in version 2, and later changes chiefly affect evidence, appendices, attribution, and rights text.

The work directly names recurrent encoder–decoders, Bahdanau-style additive attention, convolutional sequence models, earlier self-attention applications, and memory networks. Those references bound its novelty but do not make every cited work a documented causal predecessor.
Versions 5–7 do not explain whether 41.8 and 41.0 refer to different English–French runs, scoring procedures, or an uncorrected text edit.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: Versioned experiment logs, an exact code/checkpoint mapping, or an author correction would be required to reconcile the two values.

uncertainties.note: No inspected primary record ties the released Tensor2Tensor repository to an immutable revision and every reported result condition.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A contemporaneous commit, environment lock, data manifest, checkpoints, and evaluation commands would be required for exact reconstruction.

ideas.name: Text as a dependent sequence
ideas.description: Adjacent symbol classes in observed text can have different conditional frequencies than independence would predict.

uncertainties.note: The opening treatment is intentionally limited to the vowel/consonant abstraction used in the 1913 study.

ideas.name: Language as a conditional stochastic source
ideas.description: A discrete language source emits successive symbols according to probabilities that may depend on preceding choices.

ideas.name: Neural next-character probability modeling
ideas.description: A neural predictor maps a fixed character context to estimates of the next-character distribution, allowing contexts absent from a literal lookup table to share parameters.

uncertainties.note: This mechanism is character-level and uses squared-error training plus sum normalization; it is not labeled as the word-vector softmax architecture used by Bengio et al.

ideas.name: Probability-driven lossless text coding
ideas.description: Encoder and decoder run the same sequential probability predictor so Huffman or arithmetic coding can assign shorter descriptions to more likely next characters while preserving exact recovery.

ideas.name: Neural misprediction-residual coding
ideas.description: A neural predictor selects one deterministic next character, while only mistakes and the lengths of correct runs are retained before a conventional lossless coder is applied.

uncertainties.note: This longer-manuscript-only method is kept separate from Huffman and arithmetic probability coding because it records deterministic prediction errors and explicitly does not use all conditional-probability information.

ideas.name: Entropy as sequence uncertainty
ideas.description: Conditional entropy quantifies average uncertainty about a next event when contextual information is known.

ideas.name: Increasing-order language approximation
ideas.description: Successively longer conditional contexts can produce samples with more of a language’s local statistical structure.

uncertainties.note: Order labels in the paper are preserved alongside explicit context length because they differ from some modern conventions.

ideas.name: Contextual next-symbol prediction
ideas.description: The predictability of the next character can be studied while the correct preceding text remains visible.

ideas.name: Prediction-based entropy bounds
ideas.description: The rank frequencies of next-character predictions can be related to upper and lower bounds on conditional entropy.

ideas.name: Language-model-guided decoding
ideas.description: A decoder can rank candidate word sequences by combining their language-model probability with the likelihood of the observed signal.

ideas.name: Corpus-estimated language model
ideas.description: A structured sequence model can obtain transition probabilities from counts over a domain corpus.

ideas.name: Sparse language-model estimation
ideas.description: A finite sample can leave plausible sequence transitions with zero observed or expected counts, so an estimated probability of zero need not mark an impossible transition.

ideas.name: Interpolated transition estimation
ideas.description: A transition estimate can blend a detailed distribution with a more broadly tied distribution, with the mixing weight reflecting their relative reliability.

ideas.name: Deleted estimation
ideas.description: A block is evaluated as if unseen while estimation is intended to rely on retained observations, making the tuning target resemble future prediction more closely than training-data fit; practical shortcuts can retain implicit full-data dependence.

ideas.name: Word-trigram language modeling
ideas.description: A corpus-derived trigram model assigns probabilities to local three-word patterns, but finite training data leave many patterns unobserved even at million-word scale.

uncertainties.note: The idea is scoped to the chapter’s Laser Patent Text example and is not treated as evidence about unrestricted corpora.

ideas.name: Frequency-of-frequencies discounting
ideas.description: Counts of how many event types occur once, twice, and so on can adjust unreliable low counts and estimate how much total probability should remain for unseen events.

uncertainties.note: Katz attributes the adjusted-count estimator to Turing through Good’s 1953 paper; the corpus does not treat it as Katz’s invention.

ideas.name: Recursive m-gram backoff
ideas.description: A higher-order m-gram model can use a seen-event estimate directly and send unseen events to a normalized lower-order distribution. Katz makes that estimator recursive with an explicit reserved-mass calculation; Kneser and Ney preserve the seen/unseen structure while redesigning the fallback distribution.

uncertainties.note: In Katz’s estimator, this is a zero-estimate gate, not interpolation across all orders; α rescales the lower-order distribution over eligible unseen continuations to the reserved mass β̃ rather than acting as a convex mixture weight.

The papers reuse Greek letters for different quantities: Katz’s α is a lower-order multiplier and β̃ is reserved mass, whereas Kneser and Ney’s α is the seen-event estimate, β is the fallback distribution, and γ is its normalizer.

ideas.name: Context-diversity backoff distributions
ideas.description: A lower-order distribution can depend on how many distinct detailed contexts contain the observed continuation, or on how many such context–continuation events are singletons, rather than on the continuation’s raw token frequency. The original paper uses it for backoff; later work also interpolates it into seen-event estimates.

uncertainties.note: The distinct-context equation is the original paper’s marginal-constraint backoff distribution; later interpolated and modified Kneser–Ney estimators add mechanisms not present in this record.

ideas.name: Interpolated Kneser–Ney smoothing
ideas.description: A discounted higher-order n-gram estimate is recursively added to a scaled continuation-based lower-order distribution for every continuation, so lower-order evidence contributes to both seen and unseen events.

uncertainties.note: Interpolation is a later formulation: the 1995 Kneser–Ney paper applies its optimized lower-order distribution through a seen/unseen backoff gate.

ideas.name: Modified Kneser–Ney count-dependent discounts
ideas.description: Each n-gram order can use separate absolute discounts for events observed once, twice, and three or more times, with the interpolation weight returning the total removed mass through the continuation distribution.

uncertainties.note: The three discount tiers, interpolation choice, and parameter-estimation choice remain separate properties; “modified Kneser–Ney” must not be reduced to any one of them.
The fixed three-discount equations cite Klaus Ries through personal communication, and the journal article reports an independent two-discount proposal by Ney, Martin, and Wessel 1997.

ideas.name: Neural factorization of joint distributions
ideas.description: An ordered product of normalized conditional distributions is parameterized by a constrained neural network whose deterministic hidden units can share computation across several conditionals.

uncertainties.note: The hidden units are deterministic shared computations, not latent random variables; normalization comes from the product of normalized conditionals.

The precursor’s suggestion to represent large-domain values such as words with low-dimensional features is not treated as an implemented language model or as priority evidence for jointly learned word embeddings.

ideas.name: Low-dimensional feature encoding for large domains
ideas.description: Values of a large categorical domain can be represented through multiple low-dimensional features before applying a joint-distribution estimator; in the audited precursor this is a proposal for text, not an implemented or learned representation.

uncertainties.note: The record preserves the paper’s proposed encoding bridge without treating it as experimental language-model evidence or as priority evidence for learned word representations.

ideas.name: Jointly learned word representations
ideas.description: A shared lookup table maps each word type to a continuous vector, and those vectors are optimized together with the probability model rather than supplied as fixed external features.

uncertainties.note: The paper describes learned continuous word features and distributed representations; the atlas uses modern embedding terminology only as explanatory interface language, not as a quotation or priority claim.

ideas.name: Fixed-window feed-forward neural language modeling
ideas.description: A feed-forward network predicts the next word from a fixed window of shared word vectors, optionally combining a nonlinear hidden path with a direct input-to-output path.

ideas.name: Full-vocabulary neural normalization
ideas.description: One score per vocabulary item is exponentiated and normalized into a next-word distribution, coupling every training example to the full output vocabulary.

uncertainties.note: Mikolov et al. normalize retained word types plus one rare-word bucket, then divide that bucket’s probability uniformly among the merged rare types; this is not one separately learned output for every original rare type.

ideas.name: Class-factored neural output normalization
ideas.description: A word probability is decomposed into the probability of its assigned class and its probability within that class, reducing the number of output scores evaluated for each history.

uncertainties.note: The 2012 paper evaluates fixed word classes and discusses the square-root class-count heuristic; this idea does not imply a learned hierarchy or a modern approximate-softmax method.

ideas.name: Shortlist hybrid neural language modeling
ideas.description: A neural distribution is normalized over a frequent-word shortlist and scaled by the backoff model’s total shortlist mass, while the backoff model retains the remaining vocabulary probability.

uncertainties.note: The selected system is not a fixed linear mixture across the full vocabulary: it preserves a history-dependent shortlist mass taken from the backoff model.

ideas.name: Context-cached neural language-model decoding
ideas.description: When a decoder sequentially requests many word probabilities for the same history, the outputs already produced by one neural forward pass can be reused across those requests.

ideas.name: Neural and count-model mixtures
ideas.description: A neural next-word distribution can be linearly mixed with an interpolated n-gram distribution so their different generalization behavior contributes to one normalized predictor.

uncertainties.note: The evidence is paper-specific: Bengio et al. use fixed equal-weight neural/interpolated-trigram mixtures; Mikolov et al. report RNN/backoff weights of 0.75/0.25 plus RNN ensembles; and Sundermeyer et al. separately tune a Kneser–Ney/LSTM interpolation whose components use more than four billion versus 27 million training words. None of these results implies that mixtures always improve either component.

ideas.name: Learned distributed representations for symbols
ideas.description: A system can learn multi-unit internal patterns for otherwise discrete symbols so task-relevant regularities are encoded across several units rather than supplied as hand-written symbolic features.

uncertainties.note: This shared idea records a broad representation principle. It does not equate Hinton’s role-specific family codes, Elman’s context-dependent hidden states, Miikkulainen and Dyer’s task-learned global word-type patterns, and Bengio’s static jointly learned word lookup rows.

ideas.name: Similarity-based generalization in learned representation space
ideas.description: Learned internal geometry can expose task-relevant similarities so a model’s behavior transfers among structurally related cases rather than depending only on exact symbolic identity.

uncertainties.note: The Hinton evidence is restricted to two small isomorphic family graphs and four withheld facts; it is not broad semantic or cross-domain transfer evidence.

The Miikkulainen–Dyer evidence is restricted to supervised case-role and stereotyped script tasks; its similarity and cloning results do not establish portable word semantics or open-domain generalization.

ideas.name: Simple recurrent context memory
ideas.description: A copy of the previous hidden activation is supplied as context for the next step, making current state and output depend jointly on the current input and an iterated summary of prior processing.

uncertainties.note: The copied hidden-to-context links are fixed at 1.0; this idea must not be rendered as though every recurrent connection is learned or the paper trained with full backpropagation through time.
Miikkulainen and Dyer explicitly reuse Elman-style copied context, but recurrent FGREP predicts a stationary case-role target rather than the next word.

ideas.name: Constant-error recurrent memory
ideas.description: A recurrent cell preserves internal state and backward error along a fixed unit-weight self-connection, creating a path that avoids exponential decay or growth while that path remains active.

uncertainties.note: A protected error path is a local architectural property, not a guarantee that training will learn arbitrary long-range dependencies; both promoted works retain explicit task and evidence limits.

ideas.name: Gated recurrent memory access
ideas.description: Learned multiplicative controls regulate whether candidate information enters recurrent state, whether prior state is retained, and whether stored state affects cell output; the distinct gate and feedback mechanisms remain separately traceable.

uncertainties.note: The 1995/1997 version has input and output gates only. The 1999/2000 work adds learned retention, and the 2002 work adds cell-state-to-gate feedback; neither mechanism is attributed backward.

ideas.name: Adaptive recurrent state retention
ideas.description: A learned sigmoid gate multiplies the previous recurrent cell state, allowing data-dependent retention, gradual decay, or reset instead of a permanently fixed self-weight or an externally supplied boundary reset.

uncertainties.note: The 1999 report, ICANN paper, and 2000 journal article are grouped as versions of one work, but their exact equations, experiment coverage, weight counts, lag descriptions, and training means are not assumed interchangeable.
This mechanism controls activation-state retention; it is not parameter-level protection against catastrophic forgetting.

ideas.name: Cell-state-to-gate feedback
ideas.description: Learned peephole connections expose protected cell state directly to its gates, so input and forget decisions can inspect prior state and output decisions can inspect newly updated state even when ordinary cell output is closed.

uncertainties.note: The 2002 equations use prior state for input and forget gates and newly updated state for the output gate. Sundermeyer 2012 displays state-to-gate links but does not reproduce that update order, so implementation identity is not inferred.

ideas.name: Task-learned global distributed word lexicon
ideas.description: Backpropagated task error can update one stored distributed pattern per word and reuse that shared pattern as input, output, and inter-module communication across several supervised language-processing tasks.

uncertainties.note: The stored word pattern is global within DISPAR, but its geometry is learned for the supervised tasks and is not a context-dependent token representation or a word vector trained by language-model likelihood.

ideas.name: Modular recurrent neural language processing
ideas.description: Several recurrent networks can specialize in sentence parsing, story parsing, story generation, and sentence generation while communicating through a compatible learned lexicon and explicit case-role or script structures.

uncertainties.note: The modules are separately supervised with compatible targets and correct intermediate lexical patterns during training; the corpus does not describe DISPAR as an end-to-end learned pipeline.

ideas.name: One-hot neural bigram language modeling
ideas.description: A one-hot current-word input can feed a full-vocabulary affine softmax directly, making the network a normalized bigram estimator with no hidden representation and no context beyond one word.

uncertainties.note: The evaluated system contains no hidden units or learned word vectors; calling it neural records its optimization and softmax parameterization, not distributed representation learning.

ideas.name: Early stopping as implicit neural bigram smoothing
ideas.description: Selecting a direct bigram network before full training convergence can regularize sparse word-pair estimates; an exact count-dependent interpolation is derived only for a separate linear squared-error surrogate, while the actual softmax network's smoothing form remains unknown.

uncertainties.note: The corpus does not transfer equations (5.1)–(5.3) from the linear, no-bias, squared-error analysis to the implemented softmax likelihood model.

ideas.name: Next-item prediction as a training task
ideas.description: The observed next element supplies a local target, and pressure to predict it can make hidden state encode regularities in the preceding sequence.

uncertainties.note: For Elman’s lexical experiment this objective uses unnormalized output activations on generated sentences; it is not a softmax language-model likelihood or perplexity objective.
Mikolov et al. instantiate the next-word objective as a normalized vocabulary distribution trained with cross-entropy, but propagate only the current-step error in the main experiments.

ideas.name: Recurrent neural word language modeling
ideas.description: A recurrent hidden state combines the current word with the previous state to parameterize a normalized next-word distribution, allowing history to enter through repeated state updates rather than an explicit fixed window.

uncertainties.note: Recurrence removes an explicit finite input window but does not guarantee usable long-range memory; the target paper explicitly reports that its simple model did not capture truly long context.

ideas.name: Online neural language-model adaptation
ideas.description: A trained neural language model can continue stochastic-gradient updates while processing an ordered test sequence, adapting its parameters to recent text in a cache-like continuous space.

uncertainties.note: The method assumes locally coherent test order; the paper’s WSJ evaluation sentences are not consecutive, and its dynamic model is worse than the static model on that split.

ideas.name: Emergent contextual lexical structure
ideas.description: Hidden states induced by prediction over controlled word sequences can cluster by generator-defined lexical roles even though the input vectors themselves carry no category or meaning labels.

uncertainties.note: The plotted type averages can reflect category-dependent preceding contexts; the paper’s described token-level check is not displayed and supplies no quantitative cluster metric.

ideas.name: Character-level recurrent sequence generation
ideas.description: A recurrent model assigns a normalized probability to each next symbol from the preceding sequence and can feed sampled symbols back as inputs to generate variable-length character streams.

uncertainties.note: The paper evaluates both character and word prediction on Penn Treebank, but this idea names the character-level generative path; it does not imply coherent long-form generation.

ideas.name: Mixture-density handwriting generation
ideas.description: A recurrent network parameterizes a normalized mixture of correlated bivariate Gaussians for the next pen displacement together with a Bernoulli pen-lift probability, supporting likelihood training and stochastic trajectory generation.

uncertainties.note: The continuous density models the next pen offset and lift event; it does not transcribe characters, provide a calibrated legibility score, or isolate visual quality from sampling choices.

ideas.name: Monotonic Gaussian-mixture sequence window
ideas.description: A recurrent state emits positive amplitudes and widths plus cumulative positive location increments for Gaussian windows over an input sequence, yielding a differentiable soft read whose centers can move only forward.

uncertainties.note: The weights are positive but unnormalized, and the paper describes them as a window, window weight, or convolutional mechanism rather than attention.

Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio later compare this monotonic construction directly with weights over every source annotation; that comparison supports a lineage edge without proving derivation or sole priority.

ideas.name: Fixed-vector neural sequence transduction
ideas.description: A recurrent encoder maps a variable-length source sequence into one fixed-dimensional final representation, and a separate recurrent decoder uses that representation to produce a possibly different-length target sequence.

uncertainties.note: Fixed refers to the representation’s dimensionality, not to padded or fixed input length. Both audited decoders condition on one global source summary rather than revisiting individual encoder positions.

The architecture is a plausible information bottleneck, not a universal failure condition. Bahdanau supplies a scoped matched-family comparison and descriptive length curves, but attention, bidirectionality, and capacity change together; Sutskever’s source-reversal result remains an explicit counter-boundary.

ideas.name: Source-conditioned autoregressive decoding
ideas.description: A conditional target-sequence probability is factorized into normalized next-symbol distributions that depend on the source representation and the previously generated target prefix, with an end symbol defining variable output length.

uncertainties.note: The training factorization and approximate search procedure are distinct: a normalized conditional model does not make left-to-right beam search an exact solution to maximum-probability decoding.

ideas.name: Reset–update gated recurrence
ideas.description: A recurrent hidden unit uses a reset gate inside its candidate-state computation and an update gate to mix the preceding state with that candidate, allowing different units to adapt their effective timescales.

uncertainties.note: The paper calls this a new hidden unit rather than ‘GRU’; the atlas does not backdate later terminology or claim sole priority. Gate labels are version- and paper-specific: Cho’s canonical equation weights old state by z and candidate by 1−z, while Bahdanau’s appendix weights old state by 1−z and candidate by z.

The main v3/proceedings equation applies the reset vector before the recurrent matrix multiplication; v1 and the official attachment retain an older componentwise placement and are kept version-bound.

ideas.name: Decoder-conditioned soft attention
ideas.description: At each target step, a learned feedforward score compares the preceding decoder state with every source annotation; a source-position softmax produces differentiable weights whose weighted sum is a step-specific context vector.

uncertainties.note: The paper calls the component a feedforward alignment model and attention mechanism; the atlas describes the additive score composition without backdating later “additive attention” taxonomy as the paper’s own label.
Soft weights are trainable internal quantities over every source position, not a supervised word-alignment posterior or a guaranteed causal explanation.

ideas.name: Bidirectional source annotations
ideas.description: A forward recurrent network and a backward recurrent network are concatenated at each source position, so every position-wise annotation summarizes both preceding and following source context.

uncertainties.note: The encoder requires the complete source sequence before both directional annotations are available; the paper does not claim streaming translation.
The claim that each annotation concentrates around its own word follows the authors’ recency intuition rather than a measured locality ablation.

ideas.name: Fixed-vector source-summary bottleneck
ideas.description: Using one fixed-dimensional source summary for every target step may make it difficult for a sequence model to retain and retrieve all information needed for long inputs.

uncertainties.note: This is the paper’s conjectured diagnosis, not a universal theorem or an isolated causal result; the reported comparison changes attention, encoder directionality, and capacity together.
Each attention context cᵢ remains fixed-dimensional. The change is from one global summary reused at every target step to a fresh weighted retrieval over position-wise annotations.

ideas.name: Neural phrase-pair scoring
ideas.description: A conditional neural sequence score for each source–target phrase pair is added as a feature to a conventional log-linear phrase-based translation system rather than replacing its decoder or phrase table.

uncertainties.note: Generated phrase samples demonstrate that the conditional model can emit candidates, but full phrase-table replacement and direct sentence translation remain future work in this paper.

ideas.name: Deep LSTM sequence transduction
ideas.description: Separate multilayer LSTM networks encode a source sentence and autoregressively decode a target sentence, allowing the recurrent language-model decoder to be conditioned on an encoded source at large translation scale.

uncertainties.note: The proceedings target says it uses Graves’s LSTM formulation. The atlas records documented LSTM and recurrent-language-model ancestry without treating the target as an implementation of every earlier equation.

ideas.name: Source-sequence reversal for shorter dependencies
ideas.description: Reversing source-token order while retaining ordinary target order creates several short source-to-target computational paths, reducing the minimum lag without changing average aligned-token distance.

uncertainties.note: The measured reversal intervention and the authors’ incomplete causal explanation remain separate. Reversal is not bidirectionality, attention, or backward target generation.

ideas.name: Differentiable external-memory read
ideas.description: A query scores separately stored memory keys, a softmax turns those scores into a distribution over slots, and the weighted sum of corresponding values remains differentiable from the final task loss.

uncertainties.note: The query, input-memory vectors, and output-memory vectors are structurally comparable to query, key, and value roles, but the source calls the mechanism recurrent attention over external memory rather than Transformer self-attention.

ideas.name: Multi-hop memory retrieval
ideas.description: A retrieved value updates an internal query or state before another soft read, allowing a fixed number of retrieval-and-update steps before the externally visible prediction.

uncertainties.note: The reported aggregate trend favors multiple reads, but adding a hop does not improve every task or perplexity row monotonically.

ideas.name: Memory position and time encoding
ideas.description: Within-sentence position coefficients and learned memory-age embeddings preserve word order and relative story time that an unordered bag of stored symbols would otherwise discard.

uncertainties.note: This paper’s position encoding is attached to explicit memory records and is not evidence for inheritance of the Transformer’s sinusoidal sequence-position representation.

ideas.name: Memory-read neural language model
ideas.description: Recent words occupy explicit memory slots, and repeated content-addressed reads update a recurrent state before a vocabulary softmax predicts the next word.

uncertainties.note: The language-model application first appears in arXiv version 4; it is not transferred into the QA-only first three revisions.

ideas.name: Multiplicative cross-attention scoring
ideas.description: A decoder state scores encoder states with an unparameterized dot product or a learned bilinear form before softmax normalization and a source-side weighted sum.

uncertainties.note: Luong’s score is unscaled and evaluated inside recurrent encoder–decoder attention. Technical continuity with scaled batched QKᵀ does not establish that the Transformer authors adopted the mechanism from this paper.

ideas.name: Local windowed cross-attention
ideas.description: The decoder restricts source attention to a fixed-width neighborhood around a monotonic or learned position, trading a full-source scan for a differentiable local view.

uncertainties.note: The five-BLEU headline includes score choice and input feeding; the isolated transition from the reported global-plus-feed row to local-p/general-plus-feed is 0.9 BLEU.

ideas.name: Attentional input feeding
ideas.description: The previous attentional output is concatenated with the next decoder input so subsequent recurrent states can condition on earlier source-attention decisions.

uncertainties.note: The paper presents input feeding as an alignment-history or coverage-like aid, not as a measured guarantee that every source position is translated exactly once.

ideas.name: Recurrent intra-attention memory tape
ideas.description: At each recurrent step, the current input and prior adaptive state score earlier hidden states; one soft distribution reads aligned summaries from hidden and memory tapes, and those summaries feed the next gated state update.

uncertainties.note: The source calls this intra-attention inside a left-to-right recurrent model. The atlas keeps it distinct from recurrence-free all-position self-attention.

ideas.name: Gated inter–intra attention fusion
ideas.description: A two-sequence model combines attention over the target’s earlier states with attention over an encoded source; shallow fusion keeps those modules separate, while deep fusion gates the source summary into recurrent target memory.

ideas.name: Decomposable cross-sentence attention
ideas.description: Shared feed-forward projections score every element pair across two sequences; a softmax in each direction creates a separately aligned phrase for every element without a recurrent or convolutional encoder in the core model.

ideas.name: Attend–compare–aggregate factorization
ideas.description: Soft alignment decomposes a sentence-pair decision into independent aligned-subphrase comparisons; summing the resulting comparison vectors yields a fixed-size input for the final classifier.

ideas.name: Distance-biased feed-forward intra-attention
ideas.description: Feed-forward projections score all pairs within one sentence, learned relative-distance buckets bias the softmax, and each word is concatenated with its self-aligned phrase while position-wise computation remains parallel.

uncertainties.note: The target names Cheng’s intra-sentence-attention concept but replaces Cheng’s sequential gated tape with all-pairs feed-forward self-alignment and a relative-distance bias; the lineage edge is therefore concept-level, not equation identity.

ideas.name: Self-attention sequence mixing
ideas.description: Each sequence position forms a content-dependent weighted combination of representations from other permitted positions in the same sequence, allowing global position-to-position communication without a sequence-aligned recurrent update or nontrivial-width convolution.

uncertainties.note: The work cites earlier self- or intra-attention applications and attention-only entailment models. This idea names the Transformer’s sequence-mixing role without claiming that the paper originated self-attention.
The decoder mask prevents access to later target positions during prediction; it does not make complete autoregressive generation parallel across output steps.

ideas.name: Scaled dot-product attention
ideas.description: Query–key dot products are divided by the square root of key dimension before a softmax weights the values, limiting score scale while retaining a matrix-multiplication implementation.

uncertainties.note: The variance calculation motivates the scale under an independence/unit-variance assumption. The paper does not isolate the scaling factor in a dedicated reported ablation.

ideas.name: Multi-head attention
ideas.description: Several learned query, key, and value projections run attention in parallel; their outputs are concatenated and projected again so one layer can form multiple lower-dimensional retrieval views.

uncertainties.note: The single-head development result and selected visualizations support a bounded empirical description; they do not prove that heads always specialize, remain independent, or yield faithful explanations.

ideas.name: Position encoding without recurrence
ideas.description: Position-dependent vectors are added to token embeddings so an architecture without recurrent or nontrivial-width convolutional sequence order can distinguish and relate token positions.

uncertainties.note: Sinusoidal and learned positions have nearly equal in-distribution development scores in the reported row; the hypothesized advantage for extrapolating beyond training lengths is not tested.

ideas.name: Attention path length and within-layer parallelism
ideas.description: Layer families are compared by asymptotic work, the minimum sequential operations within a layer, and the longest computational path between positions, exposing a tradeoff between global quadratic attention and recurrent or convolutional paths.

uncertainties.note: Table 1 is an analytic comparison. It does not by itself establish hardware speed, memory use, learned dependency quality, or faster autoregressive decoding.
